speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A 2% cost adjustment is a reasonable decremental target to work on and the public sector agencies should use the exercise as impetus to review its organisation and its policy implementation, modus operandi to improve its efficiency and, importantly, as a result, to cut red tape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than go on penny-wise mode, the Ministries and agencies should look to trim down costs by way of re-engineering existing processes and streamlining workflows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thoughtful harnessing of technologies should be considered in every aspect to improve productivity and service delivery.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will benefit both the public and the public sector employees as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are excellent examples by the Public Service agencies which have done more and which have done well with less.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One example that comes to mind is the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) with regard to their efforts to simplify the tax system and their effective use of technology.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Its 24/7, one-stop self-service MyTax portal and the no-filing service offer taxpayers a hassle-free way to manage their tax returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And the taxpayers' satisfaction surveys ranked high consistently.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The concept of "no need for service is the best service" is clearly demonstrated here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If such service philosophy and strategy can be replicated extensively within the public sector, we would have made a quantum leap in not just the efficient delivery of public service but also deliver positive experience to the public.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I note that digital transformation of Government services is already on the Ministry of Finance's (MOF's) and many Ministries' to-do list.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) has also recommended to intensify digitisation and to leverage data as a key enabling asset to transform the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The sooner we become a digital nation where interacting digitally is citizens' everyday way of life, the sooner we can reap the benefits and advantages of a smart economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The public sector must be early adopters in this digitisation drive and be prepared to try out newer and innovative digital solutions to improve bureaucracy and, hence, benefit society at large.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, as we digitise, along the way, we may inevitably encounter some bugs or blind spots in the initial implementation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not uncommon to have minor glitches in new information technology (IT) rollouts for large organisations as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There may be criticism from the public and complaints for the inconvenience caused.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should take all these in our stride, learn from the mistakes, quickly rectify the gaps and continue to press on with bold and necessary digitisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would appreciate if the Minister can provide an update on the Government's digitisation efforts and the results so far.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At last year's MOF's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, Members had raised about using Government procurement to support innovation and capability-building by small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a good start and I would like to ask the Minister how we could push the frontier further to help more new startups in this area.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How would the Government agencies resource themselves to carry out such procurement in an extensive way?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For a start, the Government should lead the way to transform the delivery of Government services with digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How pervasive is the use of technology in making it easier and more efficient for businesses and citizens to interact with the Government?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My residents often share the frustrations of having to provide and submit the same data and documents for different Ministries to verify.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister what constraints the Government agencies face in sharing information among themselves and how digitalisation can contribute to the solution.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, data has been recognised as the most important asset for business success.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, how can businesses leverage data captured by the Government to build deep insights, new capabilities and solutions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the Government doing to make digital services for citizens easier to access and more convenient to use?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Common grouses I hear from the residents include difficulties to use the two-factor authentication and one-time passwords to access Government services for e-transactions, especially among the older generation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some older residents find themselves having to waste a lot of time getting hold of a customer service officer via phone to get a walk-through.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe it is a waste of productivity as well for the customer service officers who could be doing something else.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand the need for additional security measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there anything that can be done to make this more hassle-free for everyone involved?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, maybe we can have embracing digital for senior volunteers, whether they are humans or maybe bots speaking in Hokkien or Teochew in community clubs (CCs), for example, as we step up our widespread digitalisation for e-services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With regard to businesses, what is the Government doing to make it more efficient for them to transact with the Government?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are so many grants and rebates out there, so it can get overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What can be done to simplify application processes as well as time and effort taken to process the applications?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe an independent fiscal watchdog is necessary since the Government has been concerned with the rising expenditures in recent years, and the Minister for Finance raises the prospect of tax increases.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The public will be interested to know the effect of public expenditure and its actual impact on our fiscal position by an organisation independent of the Government by providing expert analysis.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe that no individual outside the Government has the expertise to analyse each year's Budget in much depth, and I believe that Parliament and Singaporeans would benefit from the in-depth analysis provided by an independent fiscal watchdog.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Such an office also helps to improve fiscal governance by holding the Government more accountable through better transparency.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There are countries that have an independent budgetary office.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister: what are the new forms of taxes that he is considering?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What are the Ministry's considerations in introducing new taxes?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If so, when is he looking to implement this increase in GST, and by how much?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is widely recognised that GST is a regressive tax that hurts the poor much more than it hurts the rich, which is why the Government has been providing GST Vouchers in an effort to correct the impact on lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, GST Vouchers do not fully offset the amount of GST paid by lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If the Minister is, indeed, considering an increase in GST before the end of the decade, I hope he can be upfront with Singaporeans now so that they are not blindsided by the Government, as they were with the sudden 30% increase in water price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Typically, more workers are retrenched in the first and fourth quarters of each year than in the second and third quarters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that these workers would have earned enough income to be taxed, and their tax liability becomes an additional drain on savings that they have to factor in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The six-month deferment would be in line with the duration used in labour policy for retrenchments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Giving laid-off workers the option of deferring payment of their personal income tax would help to alleviate some financial stress, especially for middle-class workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will give them room to plan their finances so that their families can be better prepared to tide over the period of unemployment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will also give them some psychological security during the transitional period to focus their energies on training and seeking re-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, Singapore has one of the most competitive tax regimes in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Together with our infrastructural quality and skilled workforce, this has enabled us to attract significant amounts of foreign direct investments (FDIs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Usually, we would consider economies, such as Hong Kong and Luxembourg, as being more comparable as competitors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The tax rates in major economies, such as the US, UK and Japan, have always been much higher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It could spark similar moves by other economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Intensified tax competition from large economies will increase the number of economies which investors consider in deciding where to put their money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Ministry's strategy should such a scenario unfold?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How severely would a US tax cut affect our ability to maintain a sustainable tax regime?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Often, such transitions happen when the individual is in his 40s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many examples of such appointments in the past, and some are also still currently serving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young people contemplating a career in the Civil Service and Armed Forces would know that there is a pathway to enable them to move into the private sector should they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, has MOF considered if this benefit outweighs the potential downside, which is that our GLCs' senior posts may be filled by individuals who lack experience in their respective industries?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has MOF analysed the performance of GLCs during periods when they are headed by a former civil servant or army officer versus periods when they are headed by an industry veteran or a private sector veteran to see if there are any differences in business performance and organisational effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, would the Ministry consider doing such an analysis?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does MOF track the amount of corporate regulation, for example, how long it takes to fill up a form, how many forms or steps are needed to attain a specific administrative objective?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And is there an active effort to minimise and streamline red tape?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, Government procurement policies impact our businesses, especially the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Is there more that the Government can do to ensure that Government procurement contracts, especially those related to construction, maintenance and transportation that usually go beyond hundreds and millions, are not unnecessarily big, which could have the unintended effect of crowding out SMEs from competing effectively in terms of Government procurement?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Through the Government procurement experience, SMEs get to build not only their track record, but also the capabilities they need to be competitive at home and outside Singapore in the internationalisation drive.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we complement these efforts and facilitate these outcomes by refinements or enhancements to our Government procurement practice, subject, of course, to alignment with international standards and obligations and the underlying principles of fairness, transparency and value for money.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the scope of work be more finely delineated, for example, by specific types of requirements so that different SMEs may take on different parts of the work?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This could help them enter into collaborations and form consortiums to bid for higher value contracts in the future.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we look into possible enhancements and refinements to the process that could help even more of them to do so?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Understandably, local SMEs and some startups are curious how they can contribute and be a part of the growth.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Will the Government be using more innovative methods to assess the solution providers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For these companies, can the Government provide some insights to a few aspects?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For companies which wish to subcontract specific modules or areas of supply within a mega project, will the Government provide this option instead of having the smaller companies to bid from the main contractor?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will provide better accountability and enable a fairer share of profit margins.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Do the Government agencies provide opportunities to SMEs or startups during the regular business period to demonstrate their products' and services' capability?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through this regular assessment, the SMEs which are successful in meeting base criteria could be placed on a list of preferred suppliers for potential invitation to future bids by the agencies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For projects under the Government agencies, sometimes it is difficult for new digital solutions to be directly adaptable to an existing system, even if it proves to be a better option.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Part of this could be due to sensitivity of information or compatibility of different systems, particularly those that straddle across functions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Would this result in the status quo of suppliers and lack of diversity to maximise an optimal outcome in our roadmap?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Three, impact of regulatory sandboxes and intellectual property (IP) access.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This initiative is intended to allow some relaxation of rules to promote innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is a welcome move for novel and unproven concepts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But, if faced with a situation where there is a handful of new startups with similar end markets, what are the guiding principles in the Ministries' consideration for relaxing the framework to ensure a level playing field from the onset?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Would this actually be the same basis that complicates the work for the IP intermediary under the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore to decide who can best access the associated IPs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am glad to note the strong focus on preparing SMEs for the future economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, while clearly a lot of thought has been put into medium- to long-term measures to help SMEs in the long run, I am concerned about the smaller players who may already be struggling.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I hope the Government can give SMEs more procurement opportunities to help them cope in the short term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is good news and I urge that this momentum be maintained or even improved upon.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: With bigger players and more foreign companies entering Singapore and the economy being lacklustre, I am concerned that the SMEs will falter against the stronger competition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will they be rolled out and how will they benefit SMEs?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whilst we recognise the principles of value for money, transparency and open and fair competition in our procurement process, have we seen an increase in the award of Government contracts to our SMEs?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there any specific procurement approaches that various agencies are embarking on to support innovation and growth in our industries and help the SMEs access these procurement opportunities?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope we can help our local SMEs build their track record and credibility to participate not just in our local market, but potential overseas markets as well.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This increase in opportunities will also enable the growth of job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it must be structured correctly to maximise participation from the private sectors, attracting interest from both large and small companies while remaining accountable to taxpayers' monies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry share on the range of procurement approaches that the agencies are using to maximise the positive externalities from Government-led demand as well as the measures in place to prevent abuses?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is possible, for instance, in information and communications technology (ICT) projects, where subsequent add-on solutions by other players are not possible because of the initial project design.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But there are positive externalities to building a resilient local SME ecosystem like jobs, opportunities and skills for Singaporeans at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: What measures is MOF taking in procurement so that smaller players like SMEs have a chance to participate?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Can larger projects be split into smaller tenders – right size, bite size?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Next, contractors in major Government tenders can have a certain signature.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: When evaluating tenders, does MOF consider the human resource (HR) and tripartism record of tendering companies, especially if the company may have a history of significant HR bad practices?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: After all, Madam, awarding a contract is a form of endorsement to the market and society.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have three suggestions towards fairer procurement practices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will allow service providers to factor in any cost increases.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will ensure that the workers' sense of job security is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I will try again this year with a few extra minutes added to my clock.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Many of them, especially retirees and elderly singles, need a measure of financial assistance, even though they may, at the same time, live in or own a private property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If we accept the above proposition as being true, then something has to be done about the way in which we means-test and administer assistance and social transfers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is only for Housing and Development Board (HDB) dwellers, with the amount of payout dependent on the HDB flat type.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, the U-Save vouchers and the service and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebates are only applicable to HDB dwellers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: To even qualify, applicants must be staying, not owning, in a property not exceeding an annual value of $13,000.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, grants and subsidies, such as the special outpatient clinic, foreign domestic worker grants, all of them include the annual value of the home as one of the eligible cumulative criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: WIS has been part of our social safety net since 2007.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is meant to incentivise less educated Singaporeans in the older age group to enter and stay in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Why then should this turn on what type of housing the applicant stays in as long as the other income criteria are also met?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It suggests to me that the annual value has become too much as a simple surrogate for accessing eligibility criteria for financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The annual value is frequently used as a measure of wealth, but it is really not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I am not against using accessible income or annual value as one of the indicators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But it cannot be the start point and end point for such a measure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I believe we can and should do more to refine our means-testing criteria so that it is no longer a blunt and ineffective tool.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It may be simple to administer, but it is not the most equitable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, whilst the ability to afford private housing may generally be indicative of wealth, there are clear exceptions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And these undoubtedly include a number of residents, especially elderly ones, who have no income and little savings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The landed properties in which some of them live, tend to be old and ill-maintained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And their elderly inhabitants usually struggle with their day-to-day expenses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For this group, their private or even landed houses are not indicators of wealth, but simply a home where they have lived their entire lives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They probably acquired it many years ago on very modest incomes but could never dream of being able to acquire it today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They are the classic asset-rich but cash-poor residents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Whatever "wealth" they possess is almost entirely locked up in their property and cannot be utilised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I would say it would be unrealistic to ask these persons to cash out, to unlock the value of their property by selling, uproot themselves in their golden years, depart from their daily routine, live away from the community they have grown accustomed to and their way of life just to cash out on their asset.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, in the means-test which includes the criterion for annual value, it applies, as I said earlier, irrespective of whether the resident actually owns the property or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, a person may be renting a home or even just a room in a home in a private house or apartment, or he may just be squatting at a friend's or relative's apartment on goodwill terms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In all of these cases, that person would not qualify for those programmes which consider as one of their means criteria the type of dwelling home in which they live.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But surely, we agree that renting a small private apartment or a room in that apartment does not automatically mean that that person is financially better off than an HDB dweller.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, I would argue probably worse off.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Leaving aside the fact that the $13,000 annual value is really a hypothetical value for persons who cannot or should not be made to unlock the value of their homes, it cannot be realised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The bar has actually been set pretty low.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In other words, if a person lives in a property where the annual value is higher than a 1- or 2-room HDB flat, he or she would probably not qualify for the social assistance programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And this comes on top of the fact that the annual values for properties are adjusted from time to time, based on market movements and with no correlation to that person's income status or income level.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, there is little, if any, consideration for the particular financial demands of the household in question, the individual's specific needs of the household in question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: To take a leaf out of Minister Chan's ethos when he was at the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), the critical challenge is how to ensure that today's middle income does not end up as tomorrow's bottom.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: To do that, our financial assistance and social transfers must be far more nimble and adept at identifying those who really need our help.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Again, in Minister Chan's words, "we have also to help the temporary poor, those who, for financial reasons, fall into hardship." Madam, in closing, I would just leave the House with the quote that I found in the Guardian which, I think, aptly summaries the point I am trying to make, and it goes like this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is a Guardian article in January 2013, "Means testing hurts people who are neither very rich or very poor because there is always a cut-off point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Some who are far from well-off and who would generally benefit from them are excluded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There are also many people who seem comfortable to the outside world, but who do not necessarily feel so themselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, they are frugal for fear of rainy days, not realising that the rain has already come."

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some examples are eligibility for the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) or the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While household income may generally be a good indicator of need, I am concerned that there are situations where this criterion may paradoxically penalise those who have no choice but to live together with their families because of, amongst others, their financial situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Elderly persons without incomes who live apart from their working children would likely be able to meet this criterion and be eligible for CHAS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, if they were to live together with their working children, the total household income per person may be beyond the $1,800 threshold.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such an event, they would not be eligible for CHAS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that family care and support should be the first and most important port of call.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, household income as a criterion may have an asymmetrical effect on particularly our sandwich middle-income families who live with and support their elderly parents and parents-in-law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such cases, where married couples have to support two sets of elderly parents as well as their children who all live in the same household, this may create a significant financial pressure on the couple even when the combined household income or household income per capita does not fall within the threshold amount for obtaining assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, richer families whose parents live apart from them will continue to benefit from the schemes since their elderly parents stand to receive subsidies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Support for such families, I respectfully submit, subverts the policy intent behind the schemes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Lim Swee Say, referring to the Silver Support Scheme, candidly recognises this anomaly in Parliament on 13 September 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He further postulated the possibility of migrating to a per capita family income basis at some point in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully suggest that the faster the Government migrate to a per capita family income basis as a criterion, the better.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the migration, we will get a more accurate picture of the number of families at the relevant percentile level where the schemes are supposed to kick in and provide help.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once we get a more accurate picture, we can even provide a higher level of subsidy for low-income families from the subsidies redirected from richer families whose parents live separately without increasing the budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I urge the Government to leverage data analytics to build our family trees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also further suggest that we look at the Japanese family registration system known as the "koseki".

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: In Budget 2017, expenditure on social transfers is more than six times that in 2007.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: And this growth has accelerated, with the last 10 years seeing much faster growth than a decade before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Between 1997 and 2007, expenditure on social transfers rose as a proportion of total expenditures from 1.4% to 2.6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: But the abovementioned total expenditures do not include special transfers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: The current Budget continues with a regular practice of giving payouts which benefit very large numbers of recipients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Unlike targeted schemes, because of the broad coverage, such payouts are spread very thin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Regular payouts of this sort are diffused in their impact and are not directly linked to structural outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: There is no doubt that they play an important role in easing the transition to policy changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: But if they become more or less permanent, their value for this purpose becomes diminished.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: I am not asking for all forms of short-term reliefs to be curtailed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: But we have to decide if it is a good idea for short-term relief to become more or less permanent entitlements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: We should move away from a situation where households compete for more Government handouts towards the creation of a support structure that has forward-looking objectives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Three broad topics have been raised by Members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, how the Government can help to build a stronger economy through digitalisation of Government services, procurement, corporate regulations and taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, there were queries on accountability, especially in relation to the Government's Budget and Government-linked companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, areas to finetune our social schemes and programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will address the cuts on the first topic and Senior Minister of State Indranee will take the other cuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the Government can and will play an important enabling and facilitative role.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the Budget Debate earlier, the Finance Minister mentioned the improvements in productivity growth over the recent years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are positive results and we must build on this momentum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Digitalisation efforts in the Public Service can play a role in our transformation efforts, and here I thank Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Saktiandi Supaat for their suggestions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our efforts to build a Digital Government are not new.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, they started in the 1980s when we first pushed for computerisation in a big way in the Public Service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we are continuing with this effort to more proactively use technology and data to improve our service delivery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, now, we are giving this a much bigger push with our Smart Nation efforts which Minister Vivian Balakrishnan highlighted and shared last Thursday.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our Digital Government efforts form an important part of the overall Smart Nation strategy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Here, MOF works closely with the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI), the Public Service Division (PSD), the Smart Nation Programme Office and GovTech to drive the Digital Government agenda by setting clear goals and maintaining central oversight.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These goals include enhancing the efficiency of our services and ensuring that citizens and businesses are satisfied with them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Based on a survey conducted last year, 77% of citizens said that they were very satisfied with Government digital services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In 2016, we maintained the top position on two rankings − the World Economic Forum's Global Information Technology Report Index as well as the Waseda-International Academy of Chief Information Officer (CIO) International e-Government ranking.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are international surveys which rank countries according to their efforts, results and potential in the area of Digital Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While we have done well, we should not be complacent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Advances in digital technologies are evolving rapidly and we have to keep up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Minister of State Janil Puthucheary shared yesterday at MCI's COS, we also need to ensure that our digital services do not leave the elderly and the less tech-savvy behind, and extra support must always be there to help them when they need it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example is the Silver Infocomm Initiative which helps our elderly stay connected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our aim is to make Government digital services more pervasive, more user-friendly for both businesses and citizens, young and old.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want users to be able to transact smoothly with minimal assistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we will do more to customise digital services to the needs of different stakeholders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Government agencies have already been doing this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am glad that Mr Liang mentioned just now the efforts of IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, in January this year, IRAS released the first phase of its redesigned MyTax Portal, which is more intuitive and mobile-optimised so that you can file taxes on your smartphone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of the users surveyed, 90% expressed no difficulty in accessing the services after the revamp, as compared to 40% before.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we will leverage technology to simplify and streamline online services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har mentioned just now, one inconvenience and constant bugbear that Members hear from people is that they have to submit the same data repeatedly to different Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To address this, we launched MyInfo last year which allows citizens to automatically fill up digital forms with just one click.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this will reduce the time spent filling up forms or having to submit supporting documents like the CPF statement repeatedly to different agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Later this year, all SingPass users will be able to make use of this MyInfo service to automatically prefill their basic details like the name, National Registration Identity Card (NRIC), address and contact number, as soon as an online form loads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it will be an automatic click and the information will be provided.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To extend these benefits to the commercial sector, we will embark on a pilot for citizens to use MyInfo when opening bank accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will begin in the second quarter of 2017 with the Overseas-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC), United Overseas Bank (UOB), Development Bank of Singapore (DBS) and Standard Chartered Bank.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also continue to make e-payment more convenient, seamless and user-friendly for citizens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Minister Vivian had already spoken about this earlier and our plans to enable the transferring of funds on a mobile phone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also exploring a one-stop platform for citizens to make payments to the Government through their mobile phones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This can potentially consolidate bills from different agencies, saving citizens the trouble of having to go through multiple channels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, we will continue to improve Government digital services for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This compares against the 77% satisfaction rate for citizens which I highlighted earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, clearly there is still more work that we need to do on the business side.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many businesses need to go through the process of applying for grants and Government licences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will strive to make these transactions more convenient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Business Grants Portal was announced last year during the Budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is a one-stop shop for businesses to identify and apply for the right grant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will continue to review and streamline the grant application process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For licence applications, we have rolled out LicenceOne progressively since 2014 to provide businesses with a one-stop business licensing portal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The portal contains several pro-business features, like an integrated application for multiple licences from different agencies and an integrated dashboard to check the status of applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Payment is also an important transaction for businesses and we will improve the e-payment landscape to make it more convenient for businesses to transact with the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In June 2016, the Accountant-General's Department (AGD) launched the Vendors@Gov mobile app which caters specifically to the needs of SMEs that transact frequently with the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Sixty-five percent of these businesses have since downloaded the app.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition to submitting electronic invoices to Government agencies, these businesses can also receive alerts on the status of their invoices and accounts and keep track of their projected cash flows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, within three months of the launch, we saw a 21% drop in the number of payment-related enquiries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also very proud that AGD clinched the "best mobile Government service award" at the World Government Summit last month.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me highlight how we support businesses through Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Members spoke on this issue and asked that the Government do more to support local companies, especially SMEs, through procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, Government procurement has played a useful role over the years in spurring lead demand and building capabilities in certain industries like defence and water.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But let us also remember that Government procurement must, first and foremost, abide by the key principles of fairness, transparency and value-for-money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our procurement processes are also governed by a clear set of rules, with checks and balances, calibrated to the value and risk of the purchase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a point that Ms Sun Xueling made and also about the need to have safeguards against potential abuses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In our desire to help companies, we must never compromise our principles of Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am glad, listening carefully to all the speeches made by Members, none of you has suggested doing so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Government support should not become a crutch for uncompetitive companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I remember what the former civil servant Mr Philip Yeo used to tell us about his work at the Chartered Industries of Singapore (CIS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He was Chair of CIS for many years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: CIS, Members would recall, was set up as an independent corporate entity to manufacture small arms ammunition for the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Mr Philip Yeo used to remind us, then Defence Minister Dr Goh Keng Swee was insistent that CIS be treated on an arms-length basis − it had to bid for MINDEF work in competition with other foreign suppliers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, it was forced to work hard to maintain a lean and efficient operation and it rose to the occasion and delivered good service to the SAF in competition with foreign suppliers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is the approach we should take – maintain stringent standards in Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ensure that these standards are fair, transparent and offer value for public monies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, at the same time, as we go about this work, we also build capabilities in our businesses and SMEs and give them maximum opportunities to win Government procurement tenders on their own merit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think this is a better approach than to artificially set aside a certain proportion of Government tenders for SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If Members look at the statistics, so far, our SMEs are doing quite well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, 80% of the number of contracts and about half of contract value, go to SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a respectable result even when compared to developed countries like the UK and the US.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Going forward, we will continue to do more through Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let me elaborate on some of the measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, Government agencies are making use of crowdsourcing methods to look for solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This approach is ideal for the Government to partner businesses, the community and individuals to reach out to smaller players to provide innovative solutions, which several Members spoke about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, at the recent Designathon 2017, organised by the DesignSingapore Council, there was a focus on developing solutions for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The winning team comprised students from the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), and they developed a device for converting a manual wheelchair into an electric one at a fraction of the price of a regular electric wheelchair.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another example is an idea that emerged from HDB's Cool Ideas challenge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an idea for a safer gas hob because fires caused by unattended cooking cause a significant proportion of fires in residential buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the students from Republic Polytechnic and Anglo-Chinese Junior College proposed a gas hob with a safety device that cuts off the gas supply when the flame goes out, preventing fires.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They worked with City Gas, the company, and Aerogaz, commercialised the idea and eventually brought this to market in 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, crowdsourcing is a useful platform for the Government to engage the community, small players and come up with more innovative solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, Government agencies will continue to ensure that tenders are appropriately sized to give SMEs a chance to compete for them, as suggested by Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Henry Kwek.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some contracts need to be of a large enough size for the supplier to invest in innovative solutions or technology to improve productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Only about 5% of contracts are above $1 million.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members spoke about construction projects and, when we think about construction projects, we think about the big ones entailing hundreds or even billions of dollars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, in fact, for construction contracts, about 80% of them have values that are less than $650,000 and can be carried out by contractors registered with BCA without a track record.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Eighty percent of contracts in the construction sector are less than $650,000 and contractors without track record can carry them out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More than 90% of construction contracts are less than $10 million and are accessible to the smaller players.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For some larger projects, where it is appropriate, the Government may call separate tenders for different parts of the contract or different parts of the project, giving smaller companies an opportunity to participate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the construction of a single Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) line is often carried out in many parts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Separate tenders may also be called for individual MRT stations, or MRT stations with connecting tunnels, depending on the complexity of the railway lines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Often, smaller companies will tender only for the "station" project, and then larger companies will tender for "station with tunnel" contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is already happening for MRT projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some smaller companies have also formed consortiums with others to tender for larger and more complex projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, we will help SMEs without track record to participate in Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, here, there were various suggestions made by Members, including Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Chen Show Mao, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Yee Chia Hsing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Minister Iswaran had highlighted the new scheme called Gov-PACT in MTI's COS last week.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Gov-PACT provides grants to SMEs and startups to collaborate with and undertake innovative projects initiated by Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: SMEs and startups will be funded at various stages of product and solution development for these innovative projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example is the Smart Elderly Monitoring and Alert System (SEMAS), which is now being piloted in Yuhua.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The system helps families take better care of elderly dependants by allowing them to monitor the safety of the elderly at home and sending them alerts when the mobile panic button is pressed during an emergency or when living patterns that are out of the norm are detected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a very useful system that is now being piloted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: HDB worked with the SMEs that were involved to develop the business model, paired them up with telecommunications companies (telcos) and helped to deploy the system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Hopefully, this works well in the pilot and we can scale it up in more housing estates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, we highlighted the Accreditation@IMDA scheme, which helps promising and innovative Singapore-based technology startups to establish their credentials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So far, the scheme has helped 59 companies by providing assistance to strengthen their products and advice on fundraising and business pitches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A good example of an SME that has benefited is SenseInfosys.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: SenseInfosys focuses on data fusion, analytics and fraud detection in military-grade intelligence projects in the security and maritime domains.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Its product enables enterprises to analyse data to gain timely and accurate insights to improve their operational processes and make more informed decisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, the company raised $2 million from investors to help accelerate the company's growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also introducing platforms to facilitate small players to take part in Government contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One such platform is the Government Electronic Business System (GeBIZ) Mall, which makes it easy for suppliers who want to sell to Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under GeBIZ Mall, suppliers are given electronic "shelf-space" to sell their goods and services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Each supplier can list 10 items on their online "shelf" for free.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, Government agencies can then buy directly from these suppliers if the purchases are below $5,000, or they can call for quotations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also making it easier for agencies to buy from smaller players.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows Government agencies to post small projects or tasks for IT programmers to work on, and no track record is required to participate on this platform.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these are the various things we are doing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is one more thing that we will do to promote best-sourcing practices and innovative solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Government agencies have already adopted outcome-based procurement where the desired outcomes are spelt out, giving tenderers the flexibility to propose the solution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF, for example, has been working with various Government agencies to implement outcome-based procurement in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) has been doing this for school cleaning since 2014.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, its tenders for school cleaning list the sites to be cleaned, the quality standards and the KPIs, and tenderers have the flexibility to propose an operations plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Various Ministries are also adopting outcome-based contracts for their security services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, MOM's tender for the provision of security services lists several desired performance outcomes and then invites tenderers to propose technology to optimise manpower resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the examples of technology that have been proposed include an automated self-service system for pass exchanges and a licence plate recognition system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, through such outcome-based tenders, we can encourage more innovative solutions from the private sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In situations where the results are uncertain and some experimentation is required, we are encouraging agencies to adopt a spiral contracting approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This means that the agencies will award the project in phases, starting with a more experimental phase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the initial experimental stages are successfully completed, then the subsequent phases of the projects are awarded to the same supplier to continue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One good example of this is what the Jurong Town Corporation (JTC) did with a tender to remotely manage its facilities and estates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Tenderers were not confined to any particular approach, and a spiral contracting approach was used, which started with a proof of concept to test out the solution on JTC's premises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And then, after the proof of concept, an evaluation was made to see which is the best, and then a decision made to proceed with a full rollout of the solution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that is another useful approach which more and more Government agencies are adopting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari gave several suggestions on fair procurement practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to respond to this point on policy changes that affect costs, the Government makes it a point to announce these in advance, as we have done with the introduction of PWM.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows suppliers to factor in their higher wage costs when bidding for contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If a contract had started before the announcement and would continue beyond the effective date of the new policy, MOF has asked buyer agencies to accede to requests by suppliers for mutually agreed termination to allow a fresh tender to be called.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the issue of liquidated damages, I will confirm that these are not intended to be punitive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government's procurement rules clearly require agencies to ensure that any liquidated damages imposed are commensurate with the losses suffered if the supplier fails to fulfil contractual obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we encourage the unions and suppliers to seek clarifications and give feedback to the agency involved if there appears to be unfair clauses in their tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Zainal Sapari also spoke about the Government's ability to shape labour market norms through responsible procurement, and I agree with them and the Government will do its part.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to work with service providers who are responsible employers and who adopt good HR practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, wherever possible, Government agencies will take into consideration the HR and tripartism records of tendering companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we focus on the sectors that are more at risk of cheap-sourcing and suppressed wages, like in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the Government buys only from accredited service providers that adopt the PWM for cleaners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we also proactively encourage service providers to adopt the NWC guidelines on wage increments for their employees, and to factor in wage increments in multi-year contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As mentioned at MOM's COS yesterday, we will also be putting in place further measures to safeguard the basic employment rights of outsourced workers under Government contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about capabilities in procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have started the work of building up capabilities to enable Government agencies to be smarter buyers and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this includes understanding the industry and technology well, so that we can stay on top of what the suppliers are doing and ensure that tender specifications are well crafted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these capabilities can help to minimise the likelihood of being locked-in to certain tenderers, especially to incumbent suppliers, which is a point that Ms Sun Xueling made just now as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hear Dr Tan Wu Meng raised several points about corporate regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF continually reviews our corporate regulations to ensure that they remain robust yet business-friendly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) had undertaken reviews in areas, such as the requirement on holding annual general meetings (AGMs) and filing annual returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Other than amending regulations directly, we are also cutting red tape and improving our systems and processes, to reduce compliance and regulatory transaction costs for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, Trade Facilitation and Integrated Risk-based System (TradeFIRST) is an assessment framework that Singapore Customs uses to determine the type of trade facilitation that is to be provided to a company.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another example is the revamped electronic transaction system, BizFile+, which was launched by ACRA in January 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This system has streamlined processes, removed over 100 ad hoc fees and included mobile options for key transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The enhancements will benefit 450,000 registered business entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tax-filing process will also be improved for businesses this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to review and strengthen our regulatory and governance framework so that it is more robust and transparent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will amend the Companies Act to allow companies registered in another jurisdiction to transfer their registration to Singapore, or what is also known as inward re-domiciliation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will make it easier for foreign companies to relocate their businesses here to tap on Singapore's strengths and ease of doing business.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also amend our laws to require companies and limited liability partnerships to maintain non-public registers containing the particulars of their beneficial owners, and by enhancing efforts to combat money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will strengthen our position as a trusted financial centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides updating our corporate regulations, we also want to ensure that our overall regulatory environment remains conducive to business innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As the Minister for Finance mentioned in his speech, we are creating more space for innovation through regulatory sandboxes where rules are suspended to allow for greater innovation and experimentation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And Miss Cheryl Chan is right that, in doing so, we also have to exercise judgement and make sure that we are fair to the different entities and, particularly, to ensure a level playing field that is applied to all entities that are being regulated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are also ongoing efforts by the Pro-Enterprise Panel to address regulatory concerns that businesses face.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The panel comprises both business leaders and senior public officers, and has received more than 1,900 suggestions, with over 1,000 of these leading to changes in rules or regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh proposed for opt-in tax deferment for retrenched workers for six months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I believe that this is a point that Ms Foo Mee Har had also suggested in the Budget Debate and this was addressed by the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I would just reiterate that we already allow taxpayers on IRAS' GIRO scheme to pay their income tax in up to 12 monthly interest-free instalments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A taxpayer who faces financial hardship may apply to IRAS for longer instalment plans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With regard to Mr Low Thia Khiang's query on the considerations for introducing new taxes, again, the Minister for Finance has spoken about them in his Budget Round-up Speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we would all like the Government to do more, but we must always ensure that our fiscal system is one that secures a better future for the next generation and not leave them with a bigger debt burden.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we must ensure that the overall fiscal system remains competitive, supports economic dynamism and reinforces individual effort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, whatever adjustments we make, these key principles remain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, we can continue to keep our economy growing and create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this regard, Assoc Prof Randolph Tan is right that we also have to be mindful of income tax changes in other countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Around the world, corporate income tax rates have been falling, and some countries have announced plans to further reduce their corporate income tax rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, I should add that our competitiveness is not just based on taxes alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We compete on many other factors − our quality workforce, rule of law, good corporate governance and infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All these have helped to build Singapore's reputation of trust, integrity and reliability and given businesses the certainty to invest here for the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to build on these strengths and the CFE recommendations provide clear steps for us to take over the coming years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is how we help lower- and middle-income Singaporeans to have better lives and build a society that all Singaporeans can truly benefit from.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will continue to build on this progressive system of taxes and transfers, even as we consider revenue options for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, no single command entity can drive our economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We need to forge stronger partnerships to reinforce our mutual efforts, tackle common challenges and move forward together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF and the Government agencies are committed to working with our partners in this shared effort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I believe I have addressed Members' questions on the first cut and I will leave Senior Minister of State Ms Indranee Rajah to take the others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While it is always useful to look at what other countries do, it is important to remember that what is done in one country is not always necessary or relevant to another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In determining whether to adopt institutions similar to those elsewhere, it is also important to understand the context in which those institutions were established.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The OBR was set up in the UK in 2010 and the context in which it was set up is as follows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The new Conservative Liberal Democrat coalition government had just taken over from the Labour government after the general election.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They were burdened by a huge deficit inherited from the previous government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There was little confidence in government economic and fiscal planning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This can be seen from the speech of the then Chancellor Mr George Osborne when he announced the setting up of the OBR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this is what he said: "So, today, less than a week after taking office, I want to explain some of the early arrangements for dealing with the fiscal crisis left by the last Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, let me just tell you some of the stark facts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Last year, our budget deficit was the largest ever it has been in our peacetime history.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This year, it is set to be among the largest in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: According to the IMF and the European Commission, it will be the largest in the G7 and the largest in the European Union.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the legacy of thirteen years of fiscal irresponsibility." Mr Osborne went on to highlight the urgent need to tackle the deficit and said that the first part of their approach was to boost credibility and confidence in the UK's fiscal framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In that context, he said the UK urgently needed a full, independent assessment of how bad their problem really was.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He went on to say, "Over the last 13 years, the public and markets have completely lost confidence in government economic forecasts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The last government's forecasts for growth in the economy, over the past 10 years, have, on average, been out by £13 billion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Their forecasts of the budget deficit three years ahead have, on average, been out by £40 billion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Unsurprisingly, these forecasting errors have almost always been in the wrong direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We need long-lasting change in the way we put together the budgets in this country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The final decision on the forecast has always been made by the Chancellor, not independent officials, and that is precisely the problem." Mr George Osborne's view was that a significant part of the problem in the UK was because of "the temptation to fiddle the figures, to nudge up a growth forecast here or reduce a borrowing number there, to make the figures add up and that had proved too great".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And so, there you have, in the words of the UK Chancellor, the context of the OBR and why the UK set it up − which is huge deficits and unreliable budgeting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure the long-term sustainability of our expenditures, this Government has consistently also taken the approach of preparing ahead for spending needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Budget is a good example of this approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Minister for Finance has highlighted the longer-term increase in healthcare and infrastructure needs and has signaled that we will be reviewing revenue measures to meet this expenditure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the right approach − spending prudently and effectively and growing our revenues fairly and sustainably.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have in place a strong system of fiscal rules and safeguards to ensure fiscal sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government is required to seek Parliament's approval for its expenditures during each year's Budget.
